questiontext.text:

(a) Complete the table of values for each equation.

(a) Completing the tables. Put the value of \( x \) into the equation, taking care with the signs: a negative number squared is positive, and a negative number cubed is negative.

Quadratic, \( {@qeq@} \): when \( x=-3 \), \( y = {@qsub1@} \); when \( x=3 \), \( y = {@qsub2@} \).

x\( -3 \)\( -2 \)\( -1 \)\( 0 \)\( 1 \)\( 2 \)\( 3 \)
y\( {@qv[1]@} \)\( {@qv[2]@} \)\( {@qv[3]@} \)\( {@qv[4]@} \)\( {@qv[5]@} \)\( {@qv[6]@} \)\( {@qv[7]@} \)

Cubic, \( {@ceq@} \): when \( x=-3 \), \( y = {@csub1@} \); when \( x=3 \), \( y = {@csub2@} \).

x\( -3 \)\( -2 \)\( -1 \)\( 0 \)\( 1 \)\( 2 \)\( 3 \)
y\( {@cv[1]@} \)\( {@cv[2]@} \)\( {@cv[3]@} \)\( {@cv[4]@} \)\( {@cv[5]@} \)\( {@cv[6]@} \)\( {@cv[7]@} \)

  1. The quadratic is Graph {@qgr@}. A quadratic graph is a parabola: it has one turning point, it is symmetrical about a vertical line through that point, and both ends point the same way (both up or both down). It also crosses the y-axis at \( y = {@yq0@} \), which is the constant term of \( {@qeq@} \) and the \( x=0 \) value in its table.
  2. The cubic is Graph {@cgr@}. A cubic graph has an S-shape: it has two turning points (a hill and a valley) and its two ends point in opposite directions. It crosses the y-axis at \( y = {@yc0@} \), the \( x=0 \) value in its table.

(c) Reading the roots. The roots of an equation \( f(x)=0 \) are the \( x \)-values where the graph of \( y=f(x) \) crosses the \( x \)-axis, because on the axis \( y=0 \). They are the red points in the graphs above.

  1. The quadratic (Graph {@qgr@}) crosses the \( x \)-axis at \( x={@qp@} \) and \( x={@qq@} \), so the roots of \( {@qpoly@} = 0 \) are \( x={@qp@} \) and \( x={@qq@} \).
  2. The cubic (Graph {@cgr@}) crosses the \( x \)-axis at \( x={@cr1@} \), \( x={@cr2@} \) and \( x={@cr3@} \), so the roots of \( {@cpoly@} = 0 \) are \( x={@cr1@} \), \( x={@cr2@} \) and \( x={@cr3@} \).
